candidates.statement: Like all global therapeutic product regulators, Health Canada recognizes that there are limitations in our 105 understanding of the benefits and harms of a product even after a product has been approved for marketing. It is 106 generally understood that there is a progression of knowledge about drugs and medical devices over their life-cycle 107 that is required to adequately support patient safety. Increasing this knowledge reduces the uncertainty associated 108 with the real-world benefits and harms of a product which may not be evident during the clinical trial/ 109 investigational testing phases, and can ultimately lead to improved health outcomes for Canadians. The product 110 monograph (drugs)/instructions for use (devices) is the basis of information for health care professionals on how to 111 use the therapeutic product safely and effectively. As more knowledge and experience are gained, the safety 112 information in the product labelling is modified and improved. Health Canada builds this post-market safety 113 knowledge, which is integral to effective clinical use, from several data sources, including ADR and MDI reports; 114 by reporting ADRs and MDI, patients and healthcare professionals are participating in the system that makes health 115 products safer. Drug safety issues evolve over time; the example below illustrates how one adverse drug reaction 116 report can ultimately lead to a change in the product monograph’s safety information. 117
candidates.context: Therapeutic products, such as drugs and medical devices, can save lives, reduce suffering and improve the lives of 98 Canadians. However, these products can cause serious adverse events and Canadians can be hospitalized as a result 99 of these events. This is a public health concern resulting in significant costs to the health care system as well as 100 individual impacts to Canadians. Health Canada’s monitoring of therapeutic product safety plays a vital role in 101 public health and patient safety, providing health care providers and patients with the most up-to-date knowledge on 102 product safety so as to prevent and mitigate ADRs and MDIs. 103 Toward Mandatory Reporting of Serious Adverse Drug Reactions and Medical Device Incidents by Health Care Institutions - A Consultation Paper to inform the design of the regulations 3 Figure 1: Example of how a safety issue involving rosiglitaz

candidates.statement: As part of its implementation of a new serious ADR/MDI reporting requirement under Vanessa's Law, Health 267 Canada must define the scope of health care institutions that would be subject to this requirement. 268

The scope of reportable serious adverse drug reactions and medical device incidents must be defined in regulations. 411 The mandatory reporting requirement under Vanessa’s Law was intended to increase the number of serious ADR 412 and MDI reports submitted by health care institutions to Health Canada so as to broaden the evidence base that 413 Health Canada uses to identify a new safety signal iv or confirm an existing safety signal generated from other data 414 sources. Although an increase in reports would not necessarily lead to an increase in the number of new signals, it 415 could lead to earlier validation or confirmation of a safety issue impacting the safe use of a therapeutic product by 416 the Canadian population. 417

When considering the options on the types of reportable serious ADRs and MDIs, it is necessary to balance the need 421 to maximize the scope of reportable events aimed at improving health product safety with the need to minimize any 422 unnecessary burden on health care institutions in providing reports. It is also important to acknowledge the 423 prioritization of the reporting of some types of serious ADR/MDI events that may have higher contribution to 424 product safety monitoring. 425 In consultations to date stakeholders raised the issue that it can be difficult to establish causality in order to 426 determine if a serious ADR/ MDI is reportable. As with all reporters, the information to be submitted only needs to 427 represent the suspicions of the reporter and there is no need to establish causality in order to send a serious 428 ADR/MDI report to Health Canada. 429

It is proposed that the prescribed health care institutions be required to only provide Health Canada with 433 information about a subset of serious ADRs that is in their control. Based on previous feedback received on 434 the type of reportable serious ADRs/MDIs, the subset proposed for serious ADRs would be all serious 435 unexpected ADRs in its control. The rationale for this approach is that it focuses on information that would 436 have the highest potential to add to the understanding of real world performance of drugs. As no subsets 437 were proposed for MDIs in the feedback received, it is proposed that health care institutions are required to 438 provide Health Canada with information about all MDIs v in its control; this would include MDIs with the 439 potential to cause harm if it were to recur. 440

candidates.statement: An alternative considered was to further limit the scope of the mandatory reporting requirements to a subset of 526 products within the list of products captured by the proposal above. The subset of products would be a targeted list 527 of drugs and/or devices. A targeted subset was considered because of feedback received in consultations that 528 reporting requirements should apply only to the highest priority products for safety monitoring. The targeted subset 529 of products would need to be readily identifiable to reporters and responsive to changing safety monitoring 530 priorities. 531
candidates.context: Alternative Considered: Targeted Subset of Drugs/ Devices 524 Two ways of delivering this alternative have been considered: (i) use of a ‘black triangle’ symbol or (ii) use of an incorporated by reference list.

candidates.statement: (i) ‘Black triangle’ symbol We have reviewed the recommendation in the 2015 Senate Report to consider other initiatives that have been implemented in key regulatory jurisdictions (eg. United States and European Union). An example of a relevant initiative in the European Union is that drugs requiring enhanced safety oversight must carry a ‘black triangle’ warning. The purpose of the ‘black triangle’ symbol is to enable health care professionals and patients to easily identify the products subject to enhanced safety monitoring. The ‘black triangle’ symbol is intended to highlight the need for extra vigilance on products containing the symbol and to stimulate reporting. Health Canada has considered limiting the applicable therapeutic products to a list of products that would carry a similar type of ‘black triangle’ symbol, however, preliminary policy analysis has indicated that this initiative may not be feasible in an institutional setting. This being said, Health Canada is engaging in ongoing exploration of the use of the ‘black triangle’ concept in other reporting settings such as those involving community pharmacies, and patients.
candidates.context: Two ways of delivering this alternative have been considered: (i) use of a ‘black triangle’ symbol or (ii) use of an incorporated by reference list. (ii.) ‘Incorporated by Reference’ List The second method considered for delivering alternative 1 would be through the use of an “incorporated by reference” (IBR) list. Institutions would be expected to consult this list in order to determine whether the product was within the scope of the reporting requirements. Incorporation by reference means that the list would become part of the Food and Drug Regulations. The benefit of having an IBR list is that rather than needing to amend a regulation to revise the list, the list can be changed as needed, without an amendment to the Regulations. candidates.statement: As part of its implementation of the Protecting Canadians from Unsafe Drugs Act (Vanessa's Law), Health Canada 561 needs to define the prescribed information data fields required when Canadian health care institutions report serious 562 ADRs and MDIs. Within the context of its current reporting programs, Health Canada has established a 563 comprehensive list of data elements that can be captured for both ADRs/ MDIs in Appendices B and C. In 564 consultations, many respondents commented that, because much of this information may not necessarily be 565 available or readily accessible, it would not be possible for them to provide all or even most of these data elements. 566 Health Canada was encouraged to identify a mandatory subset of only critical data fields that would support the 567 identification and validation of a safety issue. 568

candidates.statement: As part of its implementation of the Protecting Canadians from Unsafe Drugs Act (Vanessa's Law), Health Canada 669 needs to define the prescribed time in which prescribed Canadian health care institutions are required to report 670 serious ADRs and MDIs. 671

In setting an appropriate timeline for the reporting of serious ADRs and MDIs by health care institutions, Health 675 Canada is taking into account the following factors: the timeliness of reporting, the ability of the health care 676 institution to complete reports of good quality, and the burden of the timelines on health care institutions. The time 677 frame chosen needs to meet the objective of timely reporting of suspected safety issues to support Health Canada’s 678 early identification of trends and communication of safety issues associated with drugs and medical devices; in other 679 words, the time frame cannot be too long as suspected serious safety issues associated with health products and 680 devices are being reported. The time frame chosen needs to take into consideration the ability of the health care 681 institution to complete reports of good quality - consideration needs to be given to ensuring there is a reasonable 682 amount of time that is provided for the institution to gather the requisite information/elements needed for high 683 quality reports. In setting a time frame for reporting, care must be taken to ensure that no unnecessary 684 administrative burden is imposed on health care institutions. 685
candidates.context: Appropriate timelines for the reporting of serious ADRs and MDIs by health care institutions should be largely 687 determined by the amount of effort required to review and send a report to Health Canada. Some institutions may 688 require the vetting of details prior to submitting a serious ADR or MDI report, which could involve numerous 689 individuals or departments, such as the involvement of internal risk management or legal reviews. These steps are 690 done to mitigate concerns of professional liability or to confirm that there are no breaches of patient confidentiality. 691 In setting timelines, it is also necessary to consider provincial/territorial legislation on critical medication incident 692 reporting. 693

candidates.statement: ix Manufacturers are currently required to report ADRs to Health Canada within 15 days of receiving or becoming aware of this information. Manufacturers are required to report MDIs within 10 days of becoming aware of this information, where the incident has led to the death or a serious deterioration in the state of health of a patient, user or other person, or within 30 days where the incident could lead to death or a serious deterioration in the state of health of a patient, user or other person, if it were to reoccur.
